title: Amazon and Nvidia are dramatically expanding their AI partnership

questions.question: Will AWS add the planned two million NVIDIA GPUs across its global infrastructure between 2027 and 2028?
questions.why_it_matters: A deployment at this scale would be a major source of demand for NVIDIA GPUs and could support NVIDIA’s sales and position as a supplier to cloud providers. Whether AWS actually installs the planned GPUs also matters independently of total hyperscaler capital expenditure or aggregate compute-capacity additions: spending and capacity can change without AWS deploying this specific quantity of NVIDIA GPUs.
questions.why_not_already_covered: Existing questions track aggregate hyperscaler capital expenditure and capacity additions, NVIDIA’s revenue, and several other NVIDIA product or customer milestones. None asks whether AWS deploys two million NVIDIA GPUs. Aggregate capex or capacity could reach its measured outcome without AWS completing this particular NVIDIA-GPU deployment. The article gives no binding purchase commitment, so this question concerns the deployment outcome, not an assumed binding order.
questions.how_and_when_to_check: Check by December 31, 2028, an analyst check date based on the article’s stated 2027–2028 deployment window; the article does not give an exact completion date. Review AWS or NVIDIA announcements, public AWS infrastructure disclosures, and other credible reporting for evidence of the number of NVIDIA GPUs added and the deployment period. The article reports an intention, not a completed deployment.

evidence.quote: The cloud provider intends to add two million more GPUs across its global infrastructure between 2027 and 2028.
evidence.what_it_shows: The central reported plan and its scale and timeframe. It describes an intention, not a completed deployment or a confirmed binding order.
evidence.original_speaker: TechRadar journalist; no named speaker is attributed for this plan.

evidence.quote: This expansion follows an earlier pledge to add more than a million chips starting in 2026, as customer demand outpaced expectations.
evidence.what_it_shows: Provides context for the planned expansion and reports an earlier pledge and stronger-than-expected customer demand. It does not establish how many GPUs AWS has actually added or that the newer two-million plan will be completed.
evidence.original_speaker: TechRadar journalist; no named speaker is attributed for this statement.

evidence.quote: “Customers want the freedom to choose the best tools for their AI workloads, and they want confidence that everything works seamlessly together,” said Matt Garman, CEO of AWS.
evidence.what_it_shows: AWS’s CEO describes customer priorities that could support demand for AWS’s NVIDIA offerings, but does not confirm the two-million-GPU deployment.

evidence.quote: “That’s why we’ve invested deeply with Nvidia to make AWS the best place to run Nvidia AI technologies, optimizing performance across our infrastructure from networking and security to deployment. This expanded collaboration gives frontier labs, enterprises and governments even more ways to build and deploy AI on AWS.”
evidence.what_it_shows: Garman describes AWS’s investment in NVIDIA integration and the expanded collaboration, supporting the commercial rationale for the plan. He does not state that AWS has completed or firmly committed to deploying two million GPUs.

evidence.quote: Demand for accelerated computing across global cloud storage has continued to outpace projections that were made only months earlier this year.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article’s demand evidence supports the possibility of further AWS infrastructure expansion, but it is a journalist’s statement and does not quantify AWS-specific GPU demand.

evidence.quote: “Nvidia and AWS have built one of the great growth engines of the AI era, and demand is running ahead of every forecast,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia.
evidence.what_it_shows: NVIDIA’s CEO characterizes demand in the partnership as exceeding forecasts, which supports the rationale for expansion. It does not verify the GPU count or future deployment.
evidence.original_speaker: Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia.

evidence.quote: “For 16 years, we have scaled Nvidia computing in the cloud together. Now, we are expanding our partnership across the full stack — GPUs, CPUs, networking, open models and software — to make agentic and physical AI real at an unprecedented pace and scale that only AWS and Nvidia can deliver.”
evidence.what_it_shows: Huang confirms an expanded partnership spanning GPUs and other technologies, but does not confirm that the two-million-GPU plan is binding or completed.
evidence.original_speaker: Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia.

evidence.quote: Government agencies are also included in the plan, with 100,000 chips reserved for sensitive government and defense computing needs nationwide.
evidence.what_it_shows: Reports a specific allocation within the plan that could contribute to deployment demand. The article does not say these chips have been delivered or installed, or whether they are included in the two-million total.
evidence.original_speaker: TechRadar journalist; no named speaker is attributed for this statement.

evidence.quote: Such a large hardware commitment suggests both companies expect artificial intelligence spending to keep climbing well beyond today's already elevated levels.
evidence.what_it_shows: The journalist interprets the plan as evidence of expectations for sustained AI spending. This is an inference, not confirmation that the plan is a binding hardware commitment or will be carried out.

evidence.quote: Whether actual demand keeps pace with these ambitious plans will only become clear once the new infrastructure is fully operational.
evidence.what_it_shows: Explicitly cautions that demand may not keep pace and that the outcome remains uncertain until the infrastructure is operational.

judgements.reasons: The reference is the reported plan to add two million GPUs in 2027–2028, which sits at rung 1 (Yes). The plan is an intention, not a binding order or completed deployment, so I discount it; however, the stated demand, expanded AWS–NVIDIA partnership, and available deployment window make completing the planned amount the more likely outcome than not. The 100,000-chip government allocation is not evidence of additional chips beyond the plan, and the evidence does not establish that any of the two million have been installed.
judgements.implied_outcome: The evidence implies that AWS is more likely than not to add approximately the planned two million GPUs by December 31, 2028. This is a discounted forecast of the reported intention—not a claim that the deployment is already established—supported by the demand and partnership signals, with no quantified delay or cancellation to reduce the plan.

article:
Amazon is buying 2 million Nvidia GPUs for AWS data center expansion
By Efosa Udinmwen
AWS plans to add 2 million Nvidia GPUs between 2027 and 2028
Amazon Web Services and Nvidia have expanded their long-running partnership to add far more computing power for artificial intelligence workloads.
The cloud provider intends to add two million more GPUs across its global infrastructure between 2027 and 2028.
This expansion follows an earlier pledge to add more than a million chips starting in 2026, as customer demand outpaced expectations.
The companies also plan to bring new Vera-based CPUs into Amazon's cloud to support increasingly advanced AI applications.
Additional networking upgrades, including extended NVLink Fusion technology paired with custom high-bandwidth memory, aim to boost performance across large computing clusters.
Separate upgrades to Amazon's analytics service using Nvidia's cuDF software promise processing speeds nearing 3.7x faster than typical standard configurations.
The same upgrades are expected to deliver roughly a 30% improvement in price performance versus setups that rely only on standard chips.
Vector search capabilities on Amazon's search service are also improving, with index construction now completing roughly 9x quicker when run on GPUs.
Amazon's robotics division is separately working with Nvidia on simulation tools intended to speed up training for next-generation warehouse robots.
Government agencies are also included in the plan, with 100,000 chips reserved for sensitive government and defense computing needs nationwide.
"Customers want the freedom to choose the best tools for their AI workloads, and they want confidence that everything works seamlessly together," said Matt Garman, CEO of AWS.
“That’s why we’ve invested deeply with Nvidia to make AWS the best place to run Nvidia AI technologies, optimizing performance across our infrastructure from networking and security to deployment. This expanded collaboration gives frontier labs, enterprises and governments even more ways to build and deploy AI on AWS.”
Demand for accelerated computing across global cloud storage has continued to outpace projections that were made only months earlier this year.
“Nvidia and AWS have built one of the great growth engines of the AI era, and demand is running ahead of every forecast,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia.
“For 16 years, we have scaled Nvidia computing in the cloud together. Now, we are expanding our partnership across the full stack — GPUs, CPUs, networking, open models and software — to make agentic and physical AI real at an unprecedented pace and scale that only AWS and Nvidia can deliver.”
New processors delivered under the expanded plan are expected to offer notably faster inference and improved graphics performance for customers.
Recent hardware upgrades already deliver up to 4.6x faster inference and 2.1x stronger graphics output than the previous generation of systems.
Such a large hardware commitment suggests both companies expect artificial intelligence spending to keep climbing well beyond today's already elevated levels.
Whether actual demand keeps pace with these ambitious plans will only become clear once the new infrastructure is fully operational.
